sections.h2: Who bills and values property in Hancock County, Georgia?
sections.html:
Hancock County splits the job between two offices in Sparta. The Tax Assessor values property and handles exemptions, and the Tax Commissioner bills, collects and disburses the tax. Neither office sets the millage rate: the County Commission and the Board of Education do that each year.

Hancock is a quiet, rural county in east central Georgia. It covers 479 square miles, nearly all of it land, with Sparta as the only incorporated city and the county seat. No Interstate crosses it, and its neighbors are Taliaferro, Warren, Glascock, Washington, Baldwin, Putnam and Greene counties. The Census Bureau counted 8,735 residents in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 8,682 continues a slow slide from 9,429 residents in 2010.

  • Tax Commissioner: 9031 E. Broad Street, Sparta, 706-444-5148, Monday through Friday 9:00 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.
  • Tax Assessor: same building, 706-444-5721, open until 5:00 p.m. on weekdays.
  • Deeds: copies of a warranty deed come from the Clerk of Superior Court's deed room in the Hancock County Courthouse.

sections.h2: What are Hancock County's property tax due dates and penalties?
sections.html:
The tax commissioner's own FAQ says real estate and business personal property are due November 15 each year, and mobile or manufactured homes are due April 1. Check the date printed on your bill, because other county pages quote a different November date.

After the due date, interest runs at 1% per month on real estate and business personal property. A 10% penalty applies to any tax still unpaid 90 days after the deadline. Once taxes stay unpaid more than 30 days past due, a tax FiFa can be recorded with the Clerk of Superior Court. Those filings are public, credit bureaus can see them, and the tax office has no control over how the bureaus use them. As a last resort, the Tax Commissioner can levy on the property.

Mobile homes carry their own rules. A mobile or modular home is taxed as personal property, a return and a location permit are required, and the current year's tax must be paid in full before the permit is issued. After April 1, the county adds a 10% penalty and 1% monthly interest, and an unpaid mobile home can be sold at auction.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Hancock County assessment?
sections.html:
Send your appeal to the Board of Tax Assessors within 45 days of the date on the assessment notice. If the assessors keep their value, you can take the case to the Hancock County Board of Equalization or to an arbitrator, and after that to superior court.

The county's FAQ describes the sequence in plain terms. The Board of Tax Assessors reviews its own valuation first and tells you the result. A hearing before the Board of Equalization follows if you are still unhappy, and the Board of Equalization is appointed by the Grand Jury. Arbitration is the alternative to that hearing. A written notice to the assessors lets you continue to superior court after a decision.

Georgia taxes property at 40% of fair market value, and fair market value is set as of January 1. Only that 40% assessed portion is multiplied by the millage rate, and one mill equals $1 per $1,000 of assessed value. The assessed value is reduced by any exemption before the rate is applied. The Hancock County Tax Assessor can show you how your own parcel was valued.

sections.h2: What exemptions can Hancock County homeowners claim?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption is the main one for homeowners, and the application goes to the Tax Assessor's office. You must own and occupy the home as of January 1, and the application must arrive before April 1 to count for that tax year. Applications received later take effect the following year.

  • Once granted, a homestead exemption renews on its own while you stay in the same house. A homeowner who moves must reapply for the new address.
  • When the owner reaches age 62, the FAQ says an additional homestead exemption is available. Ask the assessor for the current forms.
  • Business owners can ask about the freeport exemption on inventory, and farm and forest owners can ask about the 10 year conservation use and preferential agricultural programs.

Property tax returns are filed between January 1 and April 1. After an initial return on real property, Georgia law renews it automatically each year at the previous value, and you file again only when you add improvements or acquire more land. A new return can also state a different value if you disagree with the current one, which starts the appeal path.

sections.h2: What do the numbers say about Hancock County homes?
sections.html:
Hancock County has some of the lowest home values in Georgia. The Census Bureau QuickFacts table puts the median owner-occupied home at $88,600 for 2020 to 2024, against a median gross rent of $938, and 79.3% of occupied homes are owner-occupied.

The gap between 5,088 housing units and 2,922 households is wide, and the 2020 census summary on Wikipedia lists 32.6% of the county's housing units as vacant. An owner of one of those houses, whether it is a family property or an inherited one, can still owe a tax bill each year. A call to the Tax Commissioner before listing shows what is owed on a parcel.

sections.h2: Who pays the tax when a Hancock County house is sold?
sections.html:
Georgia taxes the person who owns the property on January 1, so the seller usually faces the full year's bill, and the contract and closing attorney decide how it is split. Ask the Tax Commissioner in Sparta for a written payoff on the parcel before closing.

If back taxes exist, the buyer's title search will find the FiFa or any recorded lien, and the lien must be cleared at the closing table. If a lien or an unpaid mobile home tax is already in play, call 706-444-5148 early, because the Tax Commissioner has the right to levy on property that stays unpaid.

Heirs who inherit a house in Hancock County should also confirm who is named on the deed. The Clerk of Superior Court keeps the deed room in the courthouse and can supply a copy of a warranty deed, and the assessors ask first-time homeowners to bring one when they file for homestead.

faqs.q: When are Hancock County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The tax commissioner's FAQ lists November 15 for real estate and business personal property, and April 1 for mobile homes. Because other county pages show a different November date, confirm the deadline printed on your bill with the office at 706-444-5148.

faqs.q: What penalty applies to late Hancock County taxes?
faqs.a: Interest of 1% per month applies to real estate after the due date, and a 10% penalty applies to unpaid tax 90 days past the deadline. After more than 30 days, a FiFa lien can be recorded with the Clerk of Superior Court.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Hancock County assessment?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date of the assessment notice. File with the Board of Tax Assessors, then continue to the Board of Equalization, arbitration or superior court if the value stays unchanged.

faqs.q: When must I apply for a Hancock County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Apply before April 1 of the tax year in which you want relief. You must own and live in the home on January 1, and the Tax Assessor's office takes the application. A late filing starts the following year.

faqs.q: Is a Hancock County mobile home taxed differently?
faqs.a: Yes. A mobile or modular home is personal property, taxed each year with an April 1 due date. The owner needs a return and a location permit, and the current tax must be paid before the permit is issued.
